title: Support in 8 Languages? Dub the Videos, Not the Helpdesk
description: How to dub your customer support tutorials into dozens of languages and cut ticket volume — without re-recording a single screen capture.
excerpt: One tutorial video. Eight languages. A third fewer tickets.
content:
Your help center has twenty tutorial videos. All in English. And half your customers write in from Poland, Germany, and Brazil.

The result: tickets that a video would solve in two minutes get handled manually in twenty.

## Why subtitles don't cut it

Subtitles fail on tutorials. The viewer is watching a screen recording that shows exactly where to click — and simultaneously reading text at the bottom. There's nowhere to put their eyes. They miss a step, pause the video, and file the ticket anyway.

Dubbing removes the conflict. Eyes follow the interface, ears take the instruction. Exactly how it works in a native language.

## How to ship it in an afternoon

Upload the existing video to [TubeVoice](https://tubevoice.io), pick your target languages, let it run. It clones the voice from the original audio, so every language version sounds consistent — no random synthetic narrator per market.

Twenty videos × eight languages = 160 versions. Impossible by hand. This way it's one afternoon and one export.

## What to measure

Track deflection rate: the share of people who view the article-with-video and still open a ticket. After shipping localized versions, teams typically watch it drop 20–35% in non-English markets.

Second metric: median time to resolution. When the customer self-serves the walkthrough, your team only touches the real problems.

## Bottom line

Support videos are the cheapest headcount you'll ever have — always on, never paid. Give them the languages your customers actually speak. Start at [TubeVoice](https://tubevoice.io), and keep the thumbnails and attachments light with [FileTools](https://filetools.eu).
